title: Best Lovable Alternatives: 10 AI App Builders Compared for Production Apps in 2026
summary: Choosing an AI app builder for production apps means weighing trade-offs that prototyping tools never force you to confront: data connectivity, governance, code ownership, and long-term maintenance costs. If you've used Lovable and found it excellent for rapid prototyping but limiting for complex apps, backend logic, or native mobile apps,
body_text: Choosing an AI app builder for production apps means weighing trade-offs that prototyping tools never force you to confront: data connectivity, governance, code ownership, and long-term maintenance costs. If you've used Lovable and found it excellent for rapid prototyping but limiting for complex apps, backend logic, or native mobile apps, you're not alone. This guide compares the best Lovable alternatives across eight criteria that matter for teams shipping real software - not just demos. The short answer: There is no single best Lovable alternative - the right pick depends on your team profile. Developer-led teams with existing code benefit most from Cursor or GitHub Copilot. Non-technical users building business apps on existing data should evaluate Jet Admin or Bubble. For browser-based full stack generation, Bolt.new offers the closest experience to Lovable with strong code export. And enterprise teams needing governance at scale should look at platforms with built-in compliance controls and audit capabilities. How We Evaluate AI App Builder Alternatives Eight criteria separate production-ready ai app builders from tools that only shine during the initial ui drafting phase. We apply the same framework to every platform in this comparison, whether it's a visual builder, an ai coding tool, or an all in one platform. Here's why each factor matters for technical evaluators and buyers making a platform commitment: Build Speed and Development Velocity Time from natural language prompts to a working app with real functionality is the headline metric. But iteration speed matters just as much - how quickly can you add features, fix bugs, and respond to feedback? We also consider the learning curve for both developers and non technical users, since a tool that's fast for experts but baffling for business users creates bottlenecks. Data Connectivity and Integration Capabilities Production ready apps need to connect to real data: existing databases, third-party APIs, SaaS tools, and structured data sources like Google Sheets. We evaluate native database support, API integration flexibility, real-time data handling, and compatibility with existing enterprise data infrastructure. Extensibility and Customization Control Can you edit code directly? Export it to GitHub? Build custom ui components and reuse them across the same project? Code export and framework flexibility determine whether you're building on a platform or trapped inside one. Vendor lock in is the central risk here. Authentication, Permissions, and Security Built-in user management, role-based access controls, and enterprise authentication integrations (SSO, LDAP, SCIM) are non-negotiable for production apps. We also evaluate data security posture, compliance certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR), and audit capabilities. Deployment and Infrastructure Options Some teams need cloud hosting; others require on-premise or hybrid deployment. We assess hosting flexibility, scalability under production loads, DevOps integration, CI/CD pipeline support, and custom domain configuration. Governance and Enterprise Controls Version control, approval workflows, change management, and team collaboration features separate enterprise-ready platforms from solo-builder tools. Compliance certifications and enterprise security standards factor heavily here. Pricing Model and Total Cost of Ownership Transparent pricing without usage surprises matters more than headline numbers. We evaluate cost scaling with team size and application complexity, free tier generosity, paid plans structure, and long-term value compared to manual coding or hiring developers. Maintenance and Long-term Viability Platform stability, update frequency, backward compatibility, and vendor financial health all affect whether your apps will still run well in two years. Community support and documentation quality round out this criterion. Lovable Alternatives: Side-by-Side Comparison Platform Best For Starting Price Code Export Deployment Key Strength Replit Full-stack dev teams Free tier; paid plans for advanced features Yes (full code) Cloud-hosted Real-time collaboration + cloud IDE Bubble Complex no-code business apps Free tier; paid from ~$32/mo Limited Bubble cloud Mature visual platform with plugins Cursor Developer teams with existing code Free tier; Pro ~$20/mo Full (your repo) Self-managed Deep codebase awareness V0 by Vercel React UI component generation Free tier with limited generations; paid plans Full React export Vercel ecosystem Clean, production ready ui components Windsurf Budget-conscious dev teams Competitive free/paid tiers Full code access Self-managed AI assisted coding at lower cost Jet Admin Business apps on existing data Contact for pricing React code import Cloud, on-premise, hybrid Extensive data integrations + governance GitHub Copilot Universal AI code assistance Free tier; Pro ~$10/mo N/A (your code) N/A (editor plugin) Broadest IDE compatibility Base44 Rapid full-stack prototyping Starter at $20/mo for 100 message credits Limited Built-in hosting All-in-one with minimal config Bolt.new Browser-based full-stack dev Free tier with 1M tokens/month Full (ZIP/GitHub) Built-in hosting Prompt-to-app in minutes Aider Open-source AI development Free (open source) Full (your repo) Self-managed No vendor lock in, model flexibility The main takeaway: alternatives to Lovable spread across a spectrum from visual tools for non technical users (Bubble, Base44) to developer-focused ai tools (Cursor, Aider, GitHub Copilot), with platforms like Bolt.new and Jet Admin occupying productive middle ground for different use cases. Replit: Best for Full-Stack Development Teams Development velocity and real-time collaboration matter most for distributed teams that need to build, test, and deploy without local setup. Replit provides a cloud IDE for building full-stack applications, eliminating the friction of environment configuration entirely. Key strengths: Replit handles complex logic and backend workflows accurately, making it viable for production apps - not just prototypes Replit allows real-time coding and deployment in the cloud, so multiple team members can work on the same project simultaneously Replit offers a generous free tier with paid plans for advanced features like increased compute and private projects AI assistance is built into the editor, supporting ai generation of boilerplate and ai assisted app building workflows Limitations: Pricing at scale can climb quickly as compute and storage needs grow, especially for complex apps with significant traffic The learning curve for teams accustomed to traditional IDE workflows (VS Code, JetBrains) may slow initial adoption Less suited for teams that need on-premise deployment or strict infrastructure control Best for: Small teams and technical founders who want to go from idea to deployed web apps without managing infrastructure. Replit wins when collaboration speed and zero local setup are priorities. Bubble: Best for Complex Business Logic Without Code Bubble remains the most mature visual platform for building complex business apps without writing code. Its drag and drop interface, extensive plugin marketplace, and workflow engine let non technical users build surprisingly sophisticated applications. Key strengths: Visual editor with a mature drag and drop builder handles app logic, conditional workflows, and database operations without manual coding Extensive plugin ecosystem connects to external tools and services, extending functionality well beyond the core platform Proven track record with thousands of production apps running at scale Ready to use templates and reusable components accelerate development for common business app patterns Limitations: Code export is severely limited - Bubble apps are largely locked into the Bubble ecosystem, creating significant vendor lock in Performance can degrade with complex apps handling large data volumes or high concurrent user counts The learning curve is steeper than simpler no code tools because Bubble's power comes with complexity Advanced customization beyond what the visual tools support requires workarounds rather than direct code control Best for: Non-technical teams building internal tools, customer portals, or marketplace apps who accept the trade-off of limited code ownership for visual development speed. Cursor: Best for Developer-Led Teams Wanting AI Assistance For teams with existing codebases who want ai assistance without abandoning their current workflows, Cursor is the strongest option. It's a code editor with agents - not a visual builder - designed for developers who are already writing code and want AI to accelerate, not replace, their process. Key strengths: Cursor excels at maintaining complex codebases with AI assistance, understanding project context across multiple files for accurate suggestions Full code ownership is inherent: you work in your own repository, and generated code lives in your version control system Agent mode handles multi-step tasks (planning, implementing, refactoring) with human oversight, reducing boilerplate while preserving code quality Team rules enforce coding conventions and architectural decisions, supporting governance within development workflows Valued at approximately $9 billion as of mid-2026, indicating strong financial viability and continued investment Limitations: Not built for non technical users - requires coding expertise and familiarity with development environments No built-in ui generation, hosting, or deployment; you manage infrastructure externally through manual setup Less suitable for rapid prototyping of complete applications compared to visual tools like Lovable or Bolt.new Enterprise compliance certifications are less prominently documented compared to platforms built specifically for enterprise deployment Best for: Developer teams wanting to accelerate existing code workflows with ai coding capabilities. Cursor wins when full control over architecture, code visibility, and development process matters more than speed-to-first-prototype. V0 by Vercel: Best for React UI Component Generation Frontend developers who need clean, production-ready React code will find v0 by Vercel uniquely focused on their needs. Rather than generating full stack apps, V0 generates production-ready UI components with minimal adjustments needed. Key strengths: V0 by Vercel generates polished UI components ready for production - the code quality of its React and Tailwind output is consistently high Tight integration with the Vercel ecosystem means deployment is straightforward for teams already using Next.js V0 has a free tier with limited generations and paid plans that scale with usage Generated code is clean, well-structured React that developers can edit code directly and integrate into existing projects Limitations: Frontend-only focus means you need to supply or build backend logic, authentication, and database connections separately Requires technical skills to integrate V0 output into a complete application - it's a component generator, not an app builder Less useful for non technical users who need a complete working app from a single prompt No built-in hosting for complete applications (though Vercel itself handles deployment of Next.js apps) Best for: Frontend developers and design-focused teams who want ai generation of high-quality ui components that slot into existing React applications. V0 wins for UI quality but requires other tools for full stack generation. Windsurf: Best for Budget-Conscious Development Teams Cost considerations matter for small teams and startups that need ai assisted coding without enterprise-tier pricing. Windsurf offers a competitive value proposition with capable AI coding assistance at price points below most alternatives. Key strengths: Competitive pricing makes AI-powered development accessible to budget-constrained teams Full code access and code export mean no vendor lock in - you own everything you build Supports multiple AI models and provides contextual suggestions within your development workflow Lighter-weight than full-platform alternatives, reducing the learning curve for developers Limitations: Smaller feature set compared to more established platforms - fewer built-in integrations and advanced features Less enterprise focus means governance, compliance, and team collaboration features are less mature Community and ecosystem are smaller, which can affect documentation quality and third-party resource availability Not a visual builder - requires development expertise to use effectively Best for: Cost-conscious technical teams and individual developers who want solid ai coding capabilities without paying premium prices. Windsurf wins on value per dollar for teams that don't need enterprise governance. Jet Admin: Best for Business Apps with Existing Data When your data already lives in databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools, the challenge isn't generating a frontend - it's building secure business apps that connect to what you already have. Jet Admin builds secure business apps on existing data, generating the interface and application/backend logic, then deploying the app to users. Key strengths: Connects to existing databases, APIs, spreadsheets, and SaaS tools with extensive integration support - no need to migrate data to a new platform Supports prompt-based app building, importing existing React code, and AI agents that can read data, call tools, and complete multi-step tasks under permissions and audit controls Enterprise-grade security with role-based access controls, audit capabilities, and governance features designed for production deployment Deployment flexibility including cloud, on-premise, and hybrid options - critical for organizations with strict data residency requirements Limitations: Positioned as an app generation platform rather than a pure code generation tool - teams wanting raw generated code may prefer Cursor or Bolt.new Custom pricing means you need to contact sales for enterprise tiers, which adds friction to evaluation Less suited for consumer-facing web apps or marketing sites - strongest for internal tools, admin panels, and business applications Best for: Teams building business apps, internal tools, and admin panels on top of existing data sources. Jet Admin wins when data connectivity, enterprise security, and governance are higher priorities than rapid prototyping of net-new applications. GitHub Copilot: Best for Universal AI Code Assistance GitHub Copilot offers the broadest compatibility of any ai coding tool - it works across virtually every major IDE and programming language, making it the lowest-friction entry point for ai assisted coding. Key strengths: Works inside VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, and other editors - no need to switch your development environment Proven track record with millions of developers; extensive documentation and community support Cost-efficient: free tier available, Pro plans around $10/month - accessible for individual developers and small teams Accelerates writing code for repetitive tasks, boilerplate, and common patterns across any tech stack Limitations: Code assistance only - GitHub Copilot does not generate complete applications, handle deployment, or manage databases No visual editing, ui generation, or app building capabilities; it's purely a coding accelerator Less contextually aware of full project architecture compared to Cursor's deeper codebase understanding Cannot replace platform tools for teams needing full stack generation or visual builder functionality Best for: Developers who want ai capabilities embedded in their existing workflow without platform lock-in or switching costs. GitHub Copilot wins for universal accessibility but requires other tools for anything beyond writing code. Base44: Best for Rapid Full-Stack Prototyping Base44 appeals to teams that want an all in one platform for rapid prototyping with minimal configuration. Base44 manages database, hosting, and logic internally without external services, reducing setup complexity to near zero. Key strengths: Integrated backend, database, and hosting mean you can go from prompt to deployed app with minimal manual setup Base44's Starter plan costs $20/month for 100 message credits, making it accessible for early-stage projects Built-in logic and data handling reduce the need for external tools during the prototyping phase Good for quick proof-of-concept development when speed matters more than long-term architecture Limitations: Less customization and code export flexibility compared to platforms like Bolt.new or Cursor Newer platform with a smaller community - less documentation, fewer tutorials, fewer third-party integrations Advanced customization beyond what the platform supports may require migrating to a different tool Not ideal for complex apps with sophisticated backend logic or heavy external integration requirements Best for: Teams needing fast proof-of-concept development with minimal configuration. Base44 wins for speed-to-first-prototype when you don't yet need production-grade architecture. Bolt.new: Best for Browser-Based Development Bolt.new is the closest direct alternative to Lovable in terms of workflow: describe what you want in natural language, get a working app, iterate via prompt or code editor. Bolt.new generates full-stack apps from prompts in minutes, with responsive apps built by default. Key strengths: Bolt.new offers a free tier with 1M tokens/month - generous enough for meaningful experimentation Bolt.new generates readable, well-organized React code that you can export as a ZIP or sync via github integration Bolt.new offers one-click deployments and built-in hosting, eliminating deployment friction entirely Browser-based development means zero local setup - access from any machine, instantly Over 5.9 million apps created on the platform, demonstrating significant community adoption Supports integrations with Figma, Stripe, and other external tools for design-to-code and payment workflows Limitations: Scaling complexity: user reports indicate that projects can become unwieldy as dependencies and custom logic grow Mobile apps for app store submission require additional steps outside the platform - native mobile export is limited Enterprise governance features (SSO, compliance certifications, audit controls) are less visible in publicly available documentation Browser-based environment imposes constraints on resource-intensive operations compared to local development Best for: Teams that want the Lovable experience with strong code export and no local setup. Bolt.new wins for browser-based full stack generation but may require supplementing with other tools as complex apps grow. Aider: Best for Open-Source AI Development For technical teams that prioritize transparency, cost control, and freedom from vendor lock in, Aider offers an open-source approach to ai assisted coding. It runs locally, works with your existing code, and lets you choose your AI model. Key strengths: Completely free to use - no paid plans, no credit limits, no token restrictions from the tool itself (you pay only for API access to your chosen AI model) Full code visibility and code control: everything runs in your repository with standard version control Model flexibility: use OpenAI, Anthropic, local models, or any compatible provider No vendor lock in of any kind - if you stop using Aider, your code is unchanged Limitations: Requires significant technical expertise: command-line interface, local setup of development environments, and API key management No visual editing, ui generation, drag and drop building, or hosting - purely a terminal-based coding assistant Self-managed infrastructure means you handle deployment, databases, authentication, and everything else independently Smaller community compared to commercial tools, though active open-source contribution provides steady improvement Best for: Cost-conscious technical teams and individual developers who want maximum control and transparency. Aider wins for open-source ai development but demands the most technical investment of any option on this list. Which Lovable Alternative Should You Choose? Choose Replit if you need cloud-based collaboration and full-stack AI development without managing infrastructure Choose Bubble if you want visual development for complex business applications and accept limited code export Choose Cursor if you have existing codebases and want ai assisted coding with full code ownership Choose Jet Admin if you build business apps connected to existing data sources and need enterprise governance Choose V0 if you focus on React frontends with clean, production ready code and will handle backend separately Choose Windsurf if budget constraints are primary and you have development expertise on the team Choose GitHub Copilot if you want universal AI code assistance across any IDE without switching platforms Choose Base44 if you need the fastest path from idea to deployed prototype with minimal configuration Choose Bolt.new if you want the closest Lovable-like experience with strong code export and browser-based development Choose Aider if you prioritize open-source transparency and want no vendor dependencies The strongest overall recommendation for most teams evaluating alternatives to Lovable depends on your data situation. If your data already lives in existing systems, Jet Admin's integration-first approach avoids the migration pain that prompt-first builders create. If you're building net-new applications and want speed with code ownership, Bolt.new offers the best balance. And if your team is developer-heavy with existing code, Cursor provides the deepest ai assistance without forcing you onto a new platform. Migration and Selection Checklist Before committing to any platform, run through this evaluation: Technical evaluation: Audit your current databases, APIs, authentication providers, and hosting infrastructure Map which integrations are required versus nice-to-have Test whether the platform's code export produces artifacts compatible with your existing CI/CD pipelines Team skills audit: Assess your team's comfort level with writing code versus using visual tools Match platform complexity to actual team capabilities - don't buy a developer tool for a business team Consider onboarding time and the learning curve for each platform Pilot project recommendations: Start with a low-risk internal tool (time tracker, approval workflow, dashboard) rather than a customer-facing product Set a two-week timebox to evaluate build speed, integration difficulty, and deployment friction Test code export early - download or sync the generated code and verify you can run it independently Success metrics: Time to first deployed feature Cost to maintain and bug-fix over 30 days Ability to onboard a new team member to the project Whether you can export and run the application outside the platform Recommendations by Team Type and Use Case For Non-Technical Business Teams Prioritize platforms with visual editing, built-in business features, and minimal learning curve. Bubble offers the most mature visual platform for complex apps. Jet Admin is strongest when you need to build on existing data without manual coding. Base44 provides the simplest path for rapid prototyping. Documentation quality and responsive support matter disproportionately for these teams - evaluate support channels before committing to paid plans. For Developer Teams with Existing Codebases Focus on ai assistance that integrates into your current workflows. Cursor provides the deepest existing code awareness. GitHub Copilot offers the broadest IDE compatibility with the least disruption. Aider gives maximum control for teams comfortable with local setup and terminal-based workflows. Code export capabilities should be a pass/fail gate: if you can't extract and run the code independently, the tool creates risk you shouldn't accept for production ready web apps. For Enterprise Teams with Governance Requirements Prioritize security certifications, audit capabilities, role-based permissions, and deployment flexibility. Lovable itself holds SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001:2022 certifications. Jet Admin supports enterprise security with permissions, audit controls, and flexible deployment including on-premise options. Evaluate vendor stability and financial health - a tool that disappears or pivots dramatically creates migration costs that dwarf any upfront savings. Frequently Asked Questions Can these platforms replace custom development entirely? For straightforward web apps, internal tools, dashboards, and CRUD applications - yes, most of these platforms can deliver production apps without custom development. However, applications with unusual performance requirements, complex real-time systems, or highly specialized backend logic will still benefit from manual coding, at least for critical components. The practical approach is using ai app builders for 80% of the work and custom development for the remaining 20%. How do I migrate from Lovable to another platform? Lovable supports code export via GitHub sync. Export your codebase (React + Vite or TanStack Start, depending on when you created the project), then assess compatibility with your target platform. For Bolt.new or Cursor, the React code should transfer with moderate refactoring. For Jet Admin or Bubble, you're effectively rebuilding the interface on top of your data layer. Expect one to three weeks for a typical migration depending on application complexity. What's the total cost of ownership compared to hiring developers? A mid-level developer costs $80,000–$150,000/year in salary alone, plus benefits, tooling, and management overhead. AI app builder costs range from free tiers to enterprise contracts. For small teams building two to five internal tools, platform costs typically run $200–$2,000/month - a fraction of a single developer hire. The break-even favors platforms until your application complexity requires full-time engineering attention, which usually happens when you have more than 10,000 active users or complex custom integrations. How do I evaluate AI app builder security for enterprise use? Request SOC 2 Type II reports and ISO 27001 certification documentation. Verify SSO and SCIM support for your identity provider. Test role-based access controls with realistic permission scenarios. Review data residency options - where is your application data stored and processed? Check whether the platform offers audit logs that meet your compliance team's requirements. Finally, confirm the vendor's incident response process and SLA commitments. Which platforms offer the best long-term code ownership? Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Aider, and Windsurf offer inherent code ownership because you work in your own repository. Bolt.new and Lovable provide strong code export with full React codebases you can run independently. V0 by Vercel generates clean React components you fully own. Bubble offers the weakest code ownership - applications are largely locked into the platform. For maximum flexibility, choose tools where code export is a core feature, not an afterthought. Can I start with one platform and switch later? Yes, but switching costs vary significantly. Moving between code-export platforms (Lovable → Bolt.new → Cursor) is relatively straightforward because the underlying React code is portable. Moving from a no-code platform like Bubble to a code-based tool typically means rebuilding from scratch. The best strategy: choose a platform with strong code export from day one, even if you don't plan to migrate, so you preserve optionality. Ready to build production business apps on your existing data? Explore Jet Admin to see how prompt-based app building, extensive integrations, and enterprise-grade governance work together - or start with a pilot project to evaluate the platform against your specific requirements.

title: DuPont Launches DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL Chromatography Resins to Simplify Biopharmaceutical Workflows
summary: DuPont today announced the launch of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins, expanding its bioprocessing portfolio to help manufacturers streamline purification operations for oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics.
body_text: WILMINGTON, Del., April 14, 2026 — DuPont (NYSE:DD) today announced the launch of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins, expanding its bioprocessing portfolio to help manufacturers streamline purification operations for oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics. Oligonucleotide and peptide therapeutics are a growing class of targeted medicines used to treat a range of diseases—particularly genetics and rare disorders, metabolic conditions (such as diabetes and obesity), and some cancers—by precisely modulating specific biologic pathways. These therapeutics require specialized purification solutions to achieve the purity and consistency needed for clinical and commercial production. As development pipelines expand, manufacturers are increasingly focused on improving efficiency in downstream processing to support consistent quality and scalable production. The newly introduced DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins are slurried versions of the company’s existing DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT resins and are designed to simplify downstream workflows by eliminating the need for resin hydration prior to column packing. The column packing stage can require significant capital investment, including specialized equipment and additional resources, making preparation steps a key operational challenge for manufacturers. By enabling manufacturers to move directly from delivery to column packing, DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL resins help reduce preparation time, limit the need for additional equipment, and streamline purification processes, while maintaining the high resolution required for complex separations. “As oligonucleotide and peptide therapies continue to gain momentum, manufacturers are under increasing pressure to improve efficiency without compromising performance,” said Shane Kendra, Global Bioprocessing Market Leader for DuPont Water Solutions. “With the introduction of DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL resins, we are helping customers simplify downstream processing by removing time-and capital-intensive preparation steps while maintaining the purity and yield required for bioprocessing applications.” DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL chromatography resin is the smallest particle‑size resin in the DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT resin portfolio and is designed for applications that prioritize high resolution. DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT30 SL chromatography resin offers a complementary option for optimized separations at higher flow rates, providing flexibility across a range of purification and polishing steps for oligonucleotide and peptide manufacturing. DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT SL resins complement other slurried resin offerings for the company, including DuPont™ AmberChrom™ CG resins designed for chromatographic and capture applications, and DuPont™ AmberChrom™ TQ1 resin, an anion exchange resin designed for high-throughput purifications of oligonucleotides and peptides. To learn more about DuPont™ AmberChrom™ XT20 SL and XT30 SL chromatography resins and the broader DuPont bioprocessing portfolio, visit https://www.dupont.com/water/industries/life-sciences/bioprocessing.html .

title: Cómo negociar con proveedores de tecnología | Coderhouse
summary: Guía para PMs y fundadores: cómo evaluar propuestas SaaS, qué cláusulas revisar y cómo conseguir mejores precios sin sacrificar calidad ni quedar atado.
body_text: Tomás Cabiche Chief Growth Officer Negocios Cómo negociar con proveedores de tecnología: guía para PMs y fundadores de startups Publicado el 23 de julio de 2026 Contratar tecnología es hoy una de las decisiones que más define el margen de una startup. Con precios en dólares que presionan cualquier presupuesto y contratos SaaS que se renuevan solos, saber negociar con proveedores dejó de ser una habilidad "de compras" para volverse una competencia central de todo product manager y fundador. Esta guía te da un marco práctico para hacerlo bien. La buena negociación no consiste en apretar hasta el último centavo: consiste en obtener el mejor valor sostenible, con cláusulas que te protejan y una relación que puedas escalar. Vamos por partes. Antes de negociar: entendé qué estás comprando El error más caro es empezar a negociar sin claridad sobre tu propia necesidad. Antes de la primera reunión, respondé tres preguntas: ¿Qué problema resuelve realmente esta herramienta? Definí el resultado esperado, no la lista de features. ¿Cuánto vale para vos ese resultado? Ponerle un número te da tu techo de precio y tu poder de negociación. ¿Cuál es tu alternativa si no cerrás? Tener un plan B real (otro proveedor, una solución interna, o simplemente esperar) es la mayor fuente de poder en cualquier mesa. Este último punto es el famoso "BATNA" (mejor alternativa a un acuerdo negociado): cuanto más fuerte sea tu alternativa, más tranquilo negociás. Cómo evaluar una propuesta Las propuestas de proveedores tech suelen estar diseñadas para que compares mal. Para evitarlo: Calculá el costo total, no el precio de lista. Sumá implementación, onboarding, integraciones, soporte premium y crecimiento esperado de usuarios. El precio "por asiento" barato puede volverse caro al escalar. Normalizá para comparar. Llevá todas las propuestas a la misma unidad (costo anual por usuario activo, por ejemplo) para comparar peras con peras. Separá lo esencial de lo "lindo de tener". Muchos planes te cobran tiers superiores por features que no vas a usar en un año. Las cláusulas que sí importan El precio se negocia una vez; las cláusulas te acompañan todo el contrato. Prestá atención especial a: Renovación automática y aviso de cancelación: muchos contratos se renuevan solos y exigen avisar con 60 o 90 días de anticipación. Negociá plazos razonables y ponete un recordatorio. Aumentos de precio: pedí un tope de incremento anual por escrito (por ejemplo, no más de cierto porcentaje). Sin esto, quedás expuesto a subas fuertes en la renovación. Portabilidad de datos: asegurate de poder exportar tu información si te vas. Quedar "encerrado" en un proveedor por no poder llevarte tus datos es una trampa costosa. Niveles de servicio (SLA): qué disponibilidad garantizan y qué compensación hay si no cumplen. Seguridad y privacidad: especialmente crítico con herramientas de IA que procesan tus datos. La privacidad de datos figura entre los principales riesgos que preocupan a las empresas según el informe State of AI de McKinsey . Tácticas para conseguir mejor precio Sin manipular ni quemar la relación, estas palancas funcionan: Pago anual por adelantado: casi siempre desbloquea 10-20% de descuento frente al pago mensual. Timing de fin de trimestre: los equipos comerciales tienen cuotas. Negociar cerca del cierre de su trimestre suele mejorar la oferta, algo que confirman las guías de negociación de compras de Gartner . Compromiso multianual a cambio de precio fijo: útil si estás seguro de la herramienta; peligroso si no. Combinalo siempre con cláusulas de salida. Ser un caso de referencia: ofrecer un testimonio o caso de estudio puede tener valor para el proveedor y traducirse en descuento. Pedir, simplemente. La táctica más subestimada: preguntar "¿es este el mejor precio posible?" y quedarte en silencio. Sorprende cuántas veces aparece un margen. El error de mirar solo el precio Un proveedor más barato que te hace perder semanas en implementación, o que cae seguido, termina siendo más caro. Evaluá también la calidad del soporte, la solidez de la empresa y qué tan bien se integra con tu stack actual. En un contexto donde la adopción de IA crece —el 88% de las empresas ya la usa en alguna función, según McKinsey—, elegir proveedores que evolucionen contigo importa tanto como el descuento. Para equipos que operan con presupuesto ajustado, revisá también nuestra guía sobre growth marketing para startups con bajo presupuesto . Cursos recomendados de Coderhouse Negociar bien con proveedores tech requiere entender tanto el negocio como la tecnología que estás comprando. Estos programas ayudan a fortalecer ambas patas: Para tomar mejores decisiones de producto y priorización, el Curso de Product Manager te da el marco para evaluar herramientas según su impacto real. Para entender qué estás contratando cuando el proveedor vende "IA", el Curso de Introducción a la Inteligencia Artificial te permite separar el marketing de lo que la tecnología realmente hace. Y si querés reducir la dependencia de proveedores automatizando procesos internos, el Curso de AI Automation te muestra qué podés resolver sin contratar una herramienta nueva. Negociá desde el conocimiento: cuanto mejor entendés lo que comprás, mejores acuerdos cerrás. Elegí el programa que te dé esa ventaja. Preguntas frecuentes ¿Cuál es el mayor error al negociar con un proveedor de tecnología? Mirar solo el precio de lista e ignorar el costo total y las cláusulas del contrato. Un proveedor barato con mala implementación, aumentos sin tope o datos difíciles de exportar termina saliendo mucho más caro. ¿Cómo consigo un mejor precio sin arriesgar la relación? El pago anual adelantado suele destrabar descuentos, igual que negociar cerca del cierre de trimestre del proveedor. Ofrecer ser caso de referencia o simplemente preguntar por el mejor precio posible también funciona, sin necesidad de tácticas agresivas. ¿Qué cláusulas debo revisar sí o sí en un contrato SaaS? La renovación automática y su plazo de aviso, el tope de aumento anual, la portabilidad de tus datos, los niveles de servicio garantizados (SLA) y las condiciones de seguridad y privacidad, especialmente en herramientas de IA. ¿Conviene firmar contratos multianuales? Solo si estás muy seguro de la herramienta y conseguís precio fijo a cambio. Siempre acompañalo con cláusulas de salida claras y portabilidad de datos, para no quedar atrapado si tu necesidad cambia. ¿Qué es el BATNA y por qué importa? Es tu mejor alternativa si la negociación no cierra: otro proveedor, una solución interna o esperar. Tener una alternativa real y sólida es la mayor fuente de poder en cualquier negociación, porque te permite retirarte sin quedar en una mala posición. Sobre el autor Tomás Cabiche Soy Tomás Cabiche, Chief Growth Officer y Cofundador de Coderhouse. Lidero las áreas de crecimiento y marketing, impulsando la expansión de la compañía y el desarrollo de nuevos productos educativos basados en inteligencia artificial. Mi día a día combina la mirada estratégica del negocio con la ejecución, buscando siempre que la tecnología y los datos estén al servicio del crecimiento. Para conocer más sobre mi recorrido profesional, te espero en mi perfil de LinkedIn.

title: I'm a Designer. Last Week I Shipped Dark Mode to Production.
summary: How AI tooling closed the gap between design and code at Multifactor — and what it means to be a design engineer now.
body_text: I'm a Designer. Last Week I Shipped Dark Mode to Production. 2026-07-27 Company Design Agentic JB James Burns Design Engineer No ticket. No handoff doc. No waiting for an engineer to find a free afternoon. I opened the design, described what I wanted, reviewed the diff, and merged it. The whole thing went out before lunch. A year ago that sentence would have made no sense coming from me. I'm a designer — Figma is my native language, not Git. But the gap between “I designed it” and “it's live” has basically closed, and I want to walk through exactly how, because I don't think this is a James thing. I think it's where a lot of product design is heading. Dark mode, live in the Multifactor app. The old loop Here's how a UI change used to go. I'd design it in Figma. Pixel-perfect, every state, every breakpoint. Then I'd write a handoff doc — spacing, tokens, hover states, edge cases — and pass it to a frontend or full-stack engineer. They'd build it when they had bandwidth, which was rarely now . It would come back about 90% right, with the last 10% being exactly the details that make design feel designed: the easing on a transition, the way a card reflows at 380px, the contrast on a disabled state. So I'd file feedback. They'd fix it. We'd review again. The old handoff loop: the design intent and the code lived with two different people, and every round trip across that boundary cost days. Nothing here was anyone's fault. It's just that the person who held the design intent and the person who could change the code were two different people, and every round trip between them cost days. For a product like Multifactor — where the surface is a password manager people live inside, and small UI details directly shape whether the thing feels trustworthy — those days add up fast. Joining Multifactor and the moment the loop collapsed When I joined, I came in as a designer. The shift wasn't a job-title change; it was a tooling change. I started chaining together three things that, together, let me hold the design intent and change the code: Figma MCP — exposes the actual design context (variables, components, layout, tokens) from a Figma file to an AI coding agent. Instead of an engineer eyeballing my spec, the agent reads the design directly. Claude Design — where I iterate on the design itself in a canvas, conversationally, before anything touches the codebase. Claude Code — the agentic coding tool that takes the design context and the change I'm describing and produces an actual pull request against our repo. The toolchain in one shot: Figma open, Claude Code pulling design context through the Figma MCP, and a pull request opening on the other side. The unlock is the MCP connection. The design stops being a picture I describe secondhand and becomes structured context the agent can read — the same variables and components I'm working with in Figma. So “match the design” stops being a game of telephone. The receipts Theory is cheap. Here's what's actually gone to production through this workflow. Dark mode The same screen, light and dark. Dark mode is the canonical “easy for users, miserable for the codebase” feature. It's not one change — it's every surface, every token, every state, audited for contrast and consistency. The old version of me would have specced all of it and handed off weeks of work. Instead I worked through it surface by surface: iterate the theme in design, let Claude Code apply the token changes across components while reading the real design context, then review the diff like I'd review anyone's PR. The parts that needed human judgment — accessibility contrast on edge cases, a couple of components with custom states — I caught in review and corrected in the same loop. The dark mode pull request — reviewed and merged like any other. That's the receipt I care about most: dark mode went out as a single reviewed pull request that touched 55 files — +880 / −339 — the kind of change that used to mean weeks of borrowed engineering time. One concrete number beats a paragraph of adjectives. Responsiveness fixes The Multi agent chat, reflowing cleanly from a wide column down to mobile. Responsiveness bugs are the other classic handoff tax — they're invisible until you're at the exact wrong viewport, and they're tedious to describe in a ticket. Now when I spot one, I fix it where I see it. Take the Multi agent chat: the message list and the composer had to hold up from a narrow desktop column all the way down to a phone. I reproduced each breakpoint, described how it should reflow, verified it, and shipped — no ticket, no waiting. And the steady stream of small stuff A steady stream of small fixes — the kind that used to sit in a backlog forever. The headline features get the attention, but honestly the bigger change is the long tail — the spacing nits, the misaligned icons, the hover states that were never quite right. The stuff that used to sit in a backlog forever because it was never worth interrupting an engineer for. Those now just get fixed. What this did to the engineers (it's not what you'd think) The obvious-but-wrong read is “designers don't need engineers anymore.” That's not what happened, and I'd push back on anyone who frames it that way. What actually happened is that our frontend and full-stack engineers stopped building my UI work and started reviewing it. Their involvement didn't disappear — it moved to the highest-leverage point in the process. They're the final gate: they catch the architectural thing I'd miss, the performance implication, the “this should be a shared component” call. That's a far better use of a senior engineer than translating my Figma file into JSX. Review didn't go away — it moved. A real approval on one of my PRs, merged to main. So the pace on UI/UX changes went up dramatically — not because we removed people, but because we removed the round trips. The design intent and the code change now live with the same person right up until the moment of review, and engineers spend their attention where it's worth the most. What “design engineer” actually means now I used to think the line between design and engineering was about skills — that to cross it I'd need to become a “real” frontend developer. I don't think that anymore. The line was never really about skill; it was about who could act on the design directly . AI tooling moved that line, and it turns out the most valuable place to stand is right on top of it: close enough to the design to know what's right, close enough to the code to make it so. I'm still a designer. I just don't hand the design to someone else to make it real anymore. Still a designer — just no longer handing the design to someone else to make real. — James We're redefining zero-trust — so you can protect your accounts with confidence. Multifactor's provably secure zero-trust solutions cryptographically guarantee that only authorized users can access sensitive data, turning identity into your greatest asset in the fight against cyber threats. title: ServiceNow vs Resolve AI for IT Incident Automation
summary: ServiceNow & Resolve AI weren't built for lean teams. Struct deploys in under 10 min, cuts triage time by 80%, and fits Seed-to-Series C budgets.
body_text: Written by: Nimesh Chakravarthi, Co-founder & CTO, Struct Key Takeaways Startup engineering teams with 20–100 engineers face alert fatigue and slow root-cause diagnosis because enterprise tools like ServiceNow and Resolve AI assume dedicated ITSM staff. ServiceNow and Resolve AI require weeks-to-months of deployment, opaque enterprise pricing, and heavy administration that clashes with lean startup teams. Struct delivers under-10-minute deployment, Slack-native investigations, and an 80% reported reduction in triage time without ITSM expertise or infrastructure indexing. Transparent tiered pricing, SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliance, and immediate time-to-value make Struct a strong fit for Seed-to-Series C companies managing on-call rotations. Automate your on-call runbook with Struct to replace manual first-pass investigations and start reducing MTTR on day one. The Problem: Alert Fatigue and Slow Root-Cause Diagnosis in Distributed Systems On-call engineers lose 30 to 45 minutes per incident jumping between Datadog, AWS CloudWatch, Sentry, GitHub, and Slack to piece together what happened. Each investigation starts from scratch, with manual correlation of log lines, trace IDs, and recent deploys before anyone even touches a fix. The downstream impact is significant. Senior engineers lose entire sprints to firefighting instead of shipping product. Teams bound by SLAs watch resolution windows shrink with every minute spent on manual correlation. Junior engineers without deep system context escalate almost every alert, which compresses the bandwidth of the few people who understand the full system. Why This Problem Sticks Around Observability data lives in separate systems by design. Metrics sit in Datadog or Grafana, exceptions surface in Sentry, traces span cloud providers, and code context stays in GitHub. No single tool pulls these signals together automatically, so engineers do that work by hand during every incident. Tribal knowledge makes the situation worse. The one engineer who knows why a service degrades under a specific traffic pattern becomes essential during an outage and impossible to replace at scale. As the team grows, this bottleneck widens instead of shrinking. The business pays for this through elevated MTTR, SLA risk, and senior engineers stuck in reactive work instead of product development. AI-Assisted Incident Automation for Modern Teams AI-assisted incident automation covers tools that intercept alerts, gather telemetry, and surface root-cause hypotheses before an engineer starts digging. These tools fall into two main architectures: system-of-record platforms and execution-layer agents. System-of-record platforms such as ServiceNow centralize incident data, enforce governance workflows, and plug into ITSM processes. Execution-layer agents such as Resolve AI and Struct act directly on live telemetry to investigate and triage in real time. This split matters because it shapes deployment complexity, time-to-value, and how well each option fits teams of different sizes. How ServiceNow, Resolve AI, and Struct Are Built System of Record vs Execution Layer ServiceNow is a governed ITSM platform. Its AI capabilities, including AIOps and Now Assist, sit on top of a workflow engine built for change management, CMDB maintenance, and enterprise compliance. Incident automation appears as one module inside a much larger system. Configuration demands ITSM expertise, integration work, and coordination across several teams. Resolve AI operates as an agentic layer that executes remediation actions against existing infrastructure. It focuses on automating runbooks and triggering responses, but its sales motion and deployment model are enterprise-first. Teams go through scoped engagements, custom infrastructure indexing, and long onboarding cycles before they see value. Struct operates as an execution-layer agent that is Slack-native and observability-integrated. It deploys in five minutes, connects to leading observability platforms, Slack, GitHub, Linear, and Claude Code, and is fully SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant . What This Means for 20–100 Person Engineering Teams These architectural differences translate directly into operational fit for smaller teams. A 40-person engineering org does not have a dedicated ITSM administrator. It does not maintain a CMDB. It runs on Slack, PagerDuty, Datadog, and GitHub. An architecture that needs weeks of configuration before it delivers value does not work when the on-call rotation already feels stretched. See how Struct deploys in under 10 minutes using the tools your team already relies on. Evidence of Triage-Time and Ticket-Volume Reduction Struct customers working at large scale with many services report an 80% reduction in triage time. For a team where a standard investigation runs 30 to 45 minutes, that shift means investigations finish in roughly 5 to 10 minutes, often before the engineer opens their laptop. When you compare platforms, the availability of concrete metrics matters because it shows whether the vendor has validated outcomes at your scale. ServiceNow’s AIOps module reduces alert noise through event correlation and suppression, but public triage-time reduction figures for teams under 100 engineers do not exist. Its strongest value appears in organizations with mature CMDB data and established ITSM workflows. Resolve AI’s agentic remediation can automate known runbook steps, but published reduction metrics for startup-scale deployments are not available. Its architecture assumes infrastructure that has already been indexed and mapped, which adds lead time before any automation helps your team. Deployment Timelines and Ongoing Admin Work ServiceNow implementations for mid-market organizations usually require dedicated ITSM consultants, multi-week scoping, and continuous administration. The platform’s strength comes from its configurability, and that configurability consumes engineering hours and specialist attention. Resolve AI deployments involve a sales engagement, infrastructure discovery, and a scoping phase before automation starts. For teams that need relief from alert fatigue within 30 days, this schedule becomes a structural blocker. Struct setup focuses on three integration categories: an issue source such as Slack or PagerDuty, a code repository such as GitHub, and an observability platform such as Datadog, CloudWatch, GCP Logs, or similar. The full process takes under ten minutes. Auto-investigations begin as soon as connections are live. 2026 Pricing Models and Total Cost of Ownership ServiceNow pricing is contract-based and negotiated per engagement. List prices are not published. Total cost of ownership includes licenses, implementation consulting, ongoing administration, and internal engineering time to maintain integrations and workflows. Resolve AI pricing follows a similar enterprise pattern. Teams must speak with sales, and public pricing is not available. Additional costs show up in the time required to index infrastructure, design automation workflows, and keep agent configurations current as systems change. Struct publishes clear tiered pricing. A Startup tier supports up to 5 users with 30 issues per month and includes code agent handoff. A Growth tier adds unlimited users, 200 issues per month, and a build agent. An Enterprise tier adds dedicated support, volume discounts, and sidecar or on-prem support. Every tier includes a 30-day risk-free pilot with white-glove onboarding. When to Stack These Tools vs Replace Manual Work ServiceNow makes sense when an organization already runs ITSM workflows, maintains a CMDB, and wants AI layered onto existing governance processes. In that environment it becomes a stack addition, not a replacement for observability tools. Resolve AI fits organizations with mature, well-documented runbooks and infrastructure that can be indexed upfront. It acts as an execution layer that assumes operational readiness. Struct replaces the manual first-pass investigation, not the ITSM system of record. It fits teams that need immediate triage automation without months of prerequisite infrastructure work. Startup-Specific Limitations of ServiceNow and Resolve AI ServiceNow setup overhead blocks most startups. The platform was built for enterprises with dedicated IT operations teams. Deploying it at a 40-person startup demands resources the team lacks and delivers value on a schedule that does not match the urgency of on-call pain. Resolve AI enterprise friction shows up in the sales and deployment motion. Booking a demo, scoping a deployment, and waiting for infrastructure indexing to finish does not align with a 30-day decision window. The platform’s agentic capabilities are real, yet they sit behind an onboarding process designed for organizations that can invest months. If your team needs triage automation running this week, book a 15-minute Struct demo to see how quickly you can reach production value. Implementation Requirements and Data Readiness Any incident automation tool depends on the quality of the telemetry it receives. Without structured logging, trace IDs, or consistent alert configurations, the tool has no reliable signal to correlate, so teams see limited value regardless of vendor. This reality creates a clear baseline. Alerts must fire in a designated channel so they can trigger investigation. Logs must be accessible through an observability platform so they provide diagnostic context. Code must live in a connected repository so the system can attribute root causes to specific changes. Struct integrates with Datadog, Sentry, AWS CloudWatch, GCP Logs, Azure Logs and Traces, Grafana, Prometheus, Loki, Sumo Logic, Better Stack, GitHub, Slack, PagerDuty, Jira, Linear, and Asana. Teams can encode custom runbooks, correlation ID formats, and investigation instructions directly into Struct so automated investigations follow the same logic a senior engineer would apply. Neutral Evaluation Across Key Dimensions Security and compliance: Struct is SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant . ServiceNow and Resolve AI also meet enterprise compliance requirements. All three work for regulated industries at different scales. Customization: ServiceNow offers deep workflow customization at a high configuration cost. Resolve AI customizes at the runbook and agent level. Struct offers composable widgets and custom runbook encoding with minimal engineering effort. Scalability: ServiceNow scales to complex enterprises. Resolve AI scales with infrastructure maturity. Struct scales with issue volume and team size through its tiered model. Maintenance burden: ServiceNow needs ongoing ITSM administration. Resolve AI needs runbook maintenance and agent tuning. Struct needs integration authentication and occasional runbook updates. Time-to-value: ServiceNow typically takes weeks to months. Resolve AI usually takes weeks. Struct delivers value in minutes. Side-by-Side Decision Matrix for Fast Evaluation The following table brings together the main differences in setup speed, operational fit, and pricing transparency. These three factors most directly determine whether a platform can deliver value within a startup’s decision and deployment window. Criteria ServiceNow Resolve AI Struct Setup time Weeks–months Weeks <10 minutes Slack-native No Partial Yes Transparent pricing No No Yes Requires ITSM expertise Yes Partial No Enterprise compliance Yes Yes Yes Best for team size 500+ engineers 100+ engineers 20–100 engineers Custom runbook support Yes (complex) Yes (scoped) Yes (self-serve) Decision flowchart: You have a dedicated ITSM team and an existing CMDB → ServiceNow. You have mature runbooks and at least four weeks for deployment → Evaluate Resolve AI. You need triage automation running within the week, in Slack, with no admin overhead → Struct. Frequently Asked Questions Can Struct replace ServiceNow entirely? Struct automates the first-pass investigation, including root cause identification, log correlation, blast radius assessment, and suggested fixes. It does not replace a system of record for change management or CMDB. Teams that use ServiceNow for ITSM governance can run Struct alongside it to handle the triage layer that ServiceNow’s AI modules do not address at startup speed. What data quality does Struct require to function effectively? Struct relies on structured telemetry. Logs must be accessible through an observability platform, trace IDs or correlation IDs must exist, and alerts must fire into a connected Slack channel or ticketing system. Teams already using Datadog, Sentry, CloudWatch, or GCP Logs alongside GitHub are an ideal fit. Struct cannot infer system state from code alone if logging infrastructure is missing. Is Struct suitable for teams with strict compliance requirements? Struct maintains the SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliance posture mentioned earlier. Logs are accessed and processed ephemerally and are not stored persistently. For most Seed-to-Series C companies, this coverage satisfies standard security reviews. Teams with zero-egress VPC policies that block any log data from leaving internal systems should evaluate the Enterprise tier’s sidecar or on-prem option. How does Struct handle alert noise and false positives? Struct investigates every configured alert automatically and classifies it by severity and user impact. This removes the manual triage step of deciding whether an alert is a false positive, a transient blip, or a customer-facing outage. Engineers receive a pre-assessed summary instead of a raw alert, which lowers cognitive load during on-call shifts and reduces the risk of missing critical warnings. Can junior engineers use Struct effectively without deep system knowledge? Yes. Struct acts like an automated senior engineer for the first pass. It digests company-specific runbooks and produces a contextual, step-by-step starting point for every alert. Junior engineers get the same investigation depth that previously required escalation to a senior engineer, which makes it safer to expand the on-call rotation without months of onboarding. Conclusion: Choosing the Right Fit and Next Steps ServiceNow is a mature, governed platform built for enterprise IT operations. Resolve AI is an agentic automation layer built for organizations with the runway to deploy it. Both carry startup-scale limitations such as long deployment timelines, opaque pricing, and heavy administration that clash with the reality of a 40-person engineering team managing a live product under SLA pressure. Fast-growing engineering teams that need triage automation running this week require a tool that meets engineers in Slack, avoids dedicated ITSM expertise, and delivers the triage time reduction documented earlier. As Deepan Mehta, co-founder of Struct, explains, “Struct gets you from alert → root cause before you even open your laptop.” When neither ServiceNow nor Resolve AI fits the speed and scale constraints of a growing startup, Struct provides the rapid deployment mentioned earlier, Slack-native investigation, and transparent pricing with a 30-day risk-free pilot. Schedule a Struct demo to see triage automation in action .

Mark Jones, Jr. to Become President and Chief Executive Officer Effective January 1, 2027 WESTLAKE, Texas, July 22, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Goosehead Insurance, Inc. ("Goosehead" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: GSHD), a rapidly growing, independent personal lines insurance agency, today announced that Mark Miller will retire as Chief Executive Officer effective December 31, 2026. Mark Jones, Jr., currently President and Chief Operating Officer, will succeed Mr. Miller as President and Chief Executive Officer effective January 1, 2027. Mr. Miller will continue to serve on Goosehead's Board of Directors. Since joining Goosehead in 2022, Mr. Miller has led the Company through an important period of operational advancement, strengthening the executive leadership team, enhancing execution across the business, and helping position Goosehead for its next phase of growth. "Mark Miller has been an exceptional leader and partner whose impact on Goosehead will extend well beyond his tenure as CEO," said Mark Jones, Co-Founder and Executive Chairman of Goosehead. "On behalf of our Board of Directors, I want to thank Mark for his leadership, integrity, and commitment to this company. We are equally confident that Mark Jones, Jr. is the right leader to guide Goosehead into its next chapter." The leadership transition reflects the Company's long-term succession planning process. Mr. Jones, Jr. joined Goosehead in 2016 and has held executive leadership roles across finance and operations, most recently serving as President and Chief Operating Officer. Over the past decade, he has helped shape the Company's financial strategy, strengthen operational execution, and lead key strategic initiatives that support Goosehead's continued growth. "It has been a privilege to serve as Goosehead's Chief Executive Officer," said Mark Miller. "I am incredibly proud of what our team has accomplished together and grateful for the opportunity to lead this remarkable company. I have complete confidence in Mark Jr., our leadership team, and Goosehead's future." As President and Chief Executive Officer, Mr. Jones, Jr. will lead the continued execution of Goosehead's long-term strategy, with a focus on expanding the Company's technology platform, growing its distribution network, delivering exceptional client service, and creating long-term value for shareholders. "Goosehead has an exceptional team, a differentiated business model, and tremendous opportunities ahead," said Mark Jones, Jr. "I look forward to building on the momentum we've created and continuing to execute our strategy for the benefit of our clients, partners, teammates, and shareholders." body_text: Austin, Texas—Jun 11, 2026 The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has awarded Oracle a $395.8 million Federal HRIT Modernization Core Human Capital Management (HCM) contract to deliver the federal government’s first governmentwide HR platform. Powered by Oracle Fusion Cloud Human Capital Management (HCM) , the new platform will replace more than 100 separate systems and serve as the single, governmentwide system of record for workforce management under OPM’s Federal HR 2.0 initiative . Many federal agency HR systems are not interoperable. This can create duplicated efforts and inconsistent data that often results in higher costs and delays in hiring and retirement processes. By consolidating its systems onto a single cloud platform, OPM expects to reduce costs to taxpayers by more than 90 percent while strengthening efficiency, security, and service delivery for agencies and employees alike. “The federal government’s HR infrastructure has become unnecessarily fragmented, making it harder for agencies to efficiently serve employees and taxpayers. Following a rigorous, competitive evaluation process that included extensive testing and input from agencies across government, we selected Oracle Cloud HCM to help consolidate dozens of disconnected systems into a modern, secure platform,” said Scott Kupor, director, US Office of Personnel Management. “This is an important step toward improving interoperability, strengthening workforce data capabilities, and delivering a more effective and accountable HR experience across the federal government.” As the foundation for Federal HR 2.0, Oracle Cloud HCM will provide approximately two million U.S. Executive Branch civilian employees with an AI-powered, secure, FedRAMP-authorized HR platform. The solution will centralize HR operations on a single platform to improve the employee experience and effectively manage the federal workforce as a unified enterprise. Capabilities include position management, personnel action and records processing, workforce analytics, and employee and manager self-service, with integration to payroll, retirement, and benefits systems. “Oracle is honored to partner with OPM to establish a secure, trusted foundation to unify federal HR operations,” said Kim Lynch, executive vice president, Oracle Government, Defense & Intelligence. “And in doing so, we’re extending our commitment to help government leaders make faster decisions while delivering to federal employees the modern experience they deserve.” Contact Info Katie Barron Oracle Corporate Communications katie.barron@oracle.com +202-904-1138 About Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications provide an integrated suite of AI-powered cloud applications that enable organizations to execute faster, make smarter decisions, and lower costs. Oracle Fusion Cloud Human Capital Management (HCM): Provides a unified AI-powered HR platform that connects people, processes, and data to help organizations automate the employee lifecycle, enhance the employee experience, and drive better business outcomes with a human-agent workforce. Oracle Fusion Cloud Supply Chain & Manufacturing (SCM): Provides a unified AI-powered platform that integrates supply chain and operations processes and helps organizations enhance resilience and quickly adapt to market changes. Oracle Fusion Cloud Customer Experience (CX): Provides a suite of AI-powered applications that helps organizations manage marketing, sales, and service processes to win business, build stronger customer relationships, and improve customer experiences. title: Lovable Pricing Breakdown: How Does It Compare to Modelence
summary: Compare Lovable and Modelence pricing plans side-by-side. Discover which platform offers better value with our detailed breakdown of costs and features.
body_text: What You'll Pay to Keep Your App Running After It’s Ready Lovable Cloud is the second cost layer after your subscription. Your plan credits cover building with AI, but once the app is deployed, hosting is billed separately based on the resources your app uses. Lovable Cloud can include a monthly hosting allowance and a small AI allowance, but these terms may change and should be verified before publishing. The important point is that hosting is not the same thing as your Lovable plan.
